intro.paragraph: A plan YAC and the Lama Lama Rangers could carry out.

pioneering.title: The plan
pioneering.paragraph:
Implementation plan
1. Preparation. Yintjingga Aboriginal Corporation (YAC) approval would take about 6 months. The site, design and running plan are agreed with YAC and Traditional Owners. Cultural heritage checks come before any ground work.
2. Implementation. Four workers would build the shelter in the dry season in about 8 weeks, using a drill rig, steel and roof sheets. Each Ranger who will look after the site completes 4 hours of training.
3. Operation. The shelter would run during the open season, July to November (Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation [DETSI], 2024b). Rangers restock it weekly.
4. Maintenance. Two Rangers carry out two checks a year, one before and one after the wet season.
5. End of life. Four workers remove the building in 1 to 2 weeks. Shelves and kits are reused. Steel and roof sheets are recycled.

Community, ownership and evaluation
Community role: the team proposes that YAC co-designs the site and the rules, and decides which of these steps go ahead. The team encourages YAC to consider local people for the build and training.
Ownership: the team proposes that YAC owns the shelter, sets prices and decides stock. Income would help fund the Lama Lama Rangers.
Evaluation: after each open season YAC and Rangers would review kit hires, visitor numbers, empty shelves, uses of the beacons and radios, and Ranger time. They would adjust stock and prices.
Repairs: Rangers fix small faults at the weekly and twice-yearly visits. Larger repairs use local trades. YAC and Rangers should agree a repair budget.
Future: if it works, the same model could be tried at Maramba.

Other considerations
Stakeholders: YAC (owner and decision maker), Traditional Owners, the Lama Lama Rangers, visitors, Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service and Cook Shire Council. Not yet checked: land tenure and building approval, park rules for selling goods, personal locator beacon (PLB) hire rules, and insurance and liability for hired equipment. YAC should advise on each.
Visitor journey, with the main worry at each step:
1 Plan: check road conditions and park rules. Worry: will the road be open?
2 Arrive: read the safety information, buy supplies. Worry: are there enough supplies?
3 Stuck: hire a kit and recover the vehicle. Worry: cost and time.
4 Emergency: use the PLB, or the radio if coverage is confirmed. Worry: will help come?
5 Leave: return the kit and give feedback.
Ranger journey:
1 Before the season: train and stock the shelter.
2 Each week: restock and check kits.
3 Twice a year: inspect before and after the wet season.
Community reaction: The team has not yet asked YAC or Traditional Owners for their views. TEAM TO ADD: confirm this sentence is true, or add feedback received. Likely concerns are ground disturbance, extra Ranger work, visitor behaviour, theft and fire. This proposal is based on public sources and the EWB Challenge brief. It still needs to be checked with YAC and Traditional Owners.
Wider issues: waste from packaging, weeds and pests carried in firewood (use commercial bagged wood and check park rules), fire risk, theft, and wildlife safety. Safety flyers should warn visitors about estuarine crocodiles and say that swimming is unsafe. TEAM TO ADD: citation for the official crocodile warning.

Appendices
Appendix 1: Group charter. TEAM TO ADD: attach the charter before submission.
Appendix 2: Meeting minutes. TEAM TO ADD: attach the meeting minutes before submission.
Appendix 4: Full prototype test results. TEAM TO ADD: attach results before submission.
Appendix 5: Decision matrix and cost workings. The matrix scores and the cost table are shown on the Solution and Delivery pages. The contingency is 20% of $72,207.34, which is $14,441.47.

The three build lines marked Estimate (piles and stairs, design documents, shelves and solar) total $30,859.20, about 43% of the capital cost before contingency. They are the main cost uncertainty. The stock quantities are allowances sized for weekly restocking in a 22-week season. They are not measured demand. TEAM TO ADD: the basis for the stock quantities.

quotes.name: Table 2. Revenue and profit estimates (AUD)

quotes.quote: The base case assumes 10 visitors a week for 22 weeks (Todio, n.d.). Revenue is the team's estimate of hire fees plus sales of water, food and firewood. TEAM TO ADD: the revenue workings for each case, and how the low and high running costs were worked out. Two kits can be hired for at most 44 kit-weeks in a 22-week season, so the high case of 70 hires needs shorter hires or more kits. Profit is before the build cost and before Ranger time, which is not costed.
quotes.name: Revenue assumptions

quotes.quote: The team proposes a one-off grant of about $86,650 for the build and equipment. Sales and hire fees would cover stock and running costs. Regional Tourism Infrastructure Fund (Queensland): build, design and equipment, up to $300,000 (DETSI, 2026). Eligibility must be confirmed. Indigenous Rangers Program (Australian Government): Ranger land care to 2028, which may help cover Ranger time (National Indigenous Australians Agency [NIAA], n.d.). Own income: stock and about $3,950 a year to run.
quotes.name: Funding

quotes.quote: Without a grant, profit would repay the $87,387 build cost in about 46 years (low case), 17.5 years (base) or 7.7 years (high). In the low case, 25 years of profit does not cover the build. This is why the team proposes a grant for the build.
quotes.name: Payback

values.title: References and appendices
values.description: Appendix 3: Statement of AI use and prompt log. The team used generative AI in four ways. Claude (Anthropic, 2026) helped find and summarise public sources and prices, draft background and criteria text, build the cost and revenue calculations, and turn the team's slides and research into website text. Gemini (Google, 2026) made the concept images for the team's presentation. An AI image tool made the concept images on this site. An AI coding agent placed the text and images into the website. The team used AI to work faster, keep the site consistent and show the idea visually. The team chose the design, built the Blender prototype and checked figures and citations against sources. AI images are concept images, not photographs. This is a draft declaration. TEAM TO ADD: read and confirm every sentence, the exact tool names and versions, and screenshots of every prompt and output.

closing.title: What should happen next
closing.description: 1. Co-design the building, site and rules with YAC and Traditional Owners before any ground work. 2. Complete a site survey and cultural heritage clearance for the exact location. 3. Get flood level data and an engineer's design for flood and wind loads. Confirm the roof material. 4. Confirm the rules for hiring out beacons with the Australian Maritime Safety Authority, and test UHF radio coverage between Warokutal and the Ranger Base. TEAM TO ADD: citation for the beacon rules. 5. Check grant eligibility and apply. 6. Agree Ranger workload and repair budget with YAC. 7. Run a one-season trial of kit hire from the Ranger Base to test demand before building. Further research: visitor counts, local flood heights, hire demand and the price visitors will accept.
